text: Chapter 1's tagging discipline and Lesson 21's AutoShutdown tag both assume the tags are actually there. That assumption breaks down constantly in practice, and this lesson automates checking it instead of hoping it's true.

Someone provisions a VM through the portal at 11 PM without filling in the tags field. Nothing fails — the resource works exactly the same with or without it — which is exactly why missing tags go unnoticed for months. Cost analysis quietly stops attributing that resource's spend to the right project, and AutoShutdown schedules quietly skip VMs that were supposed to be included. No error, no alert — the tag is just absent, and nobody finds out until someone goes looking.

A subscription settles on a small set of required tags, commonly CostCenter and Environment. The goal isn't tagging everything with everything — it's guaranteeing these specific keys exist on every resource, so cost reporting and automation scripts that key off them never silently miss one.

The script pulls every resource and checks each one against the required tag list. ContainsKey checks for one specific key, not just whether any tags exist at all — a resource can have several tags and still be missing the one that matters. The -not $resource.Tags check catches a resource with no tags at all first, since calling ContainsKey on nothing would error out instead of reporting it as non-compliant.

A one-time cleanup pass fixes today's non-compliant resources, but new ones get created every week, and this script's entire value is catching those before they've gone untagged for months. The same runbook-and-schedule pattern from Lesson 21 applies: publish it as a runbook, attach a weekly schedule, and let it report automatically rather than waiting for someone to remember to run it.

The output is a flat list of resource name, type, and missing tag — the follow-up is the same Update-AzTag call from Lesson 21, run against each flagged resource. Next up: automating backup verification — confirming a scheduled backup actually completed, instead of assuming the schedule is working.
